subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The CMB: A Baby Photo of the Universe
description: A micro-lesson that makes The CMB: A Baby Photo of the Universe usable.

hook.text: The Cosmic Microwave Background is the oldest light in the universe—released 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

buildup.text: It's a nearly uniform glow at 2.7 K. But tiny temperature variations—one part in 100,000—reveal the seeds of all structure.

discovery.text: The COBE satellite first detected these variations in 1992. George Smoot called them 'the face of God.'

twist.text: Planck satellite measured the CMB with exquisite precision, pinning down the universe's age, shape, and composition.

climax.text: Those tiny hot spots became galaxy clusters. Those cold spots became voids. The baby photo predicted the adult universe.

punchline.text: One photo, 13.8 billion years old. The blueprint for everything.

quiz.question: What do the tiny temperature variations in the CMB represent?
options: The seeds that grew into galaxy clusters and cosmic voids
Shadows of black holes that existed at the time
Interference from other universes in a multiverse

details.summary: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the oldest light in the universe — a faint glow of microwave radiation released 380,000 years after the Big Bang when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form.
details.whyItMatters: The CMB is our most direct observation of the infant universe. It confirms the Big Bang, reveals the universe's composition (5% matter, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy), and provides the initial conditions for all cosmic structure.
takeaways: The oldest light in the universe, released 380,000 years after the Big Bang
Tiny temperature variations seeded all cosmic structure
Confirms the Big Bang and reveals the universe's composition

faq.question: How was the CMB discovered?
faq.answer: Accidentally, in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs. They detected persistent microwave noise they couldn't eliminate from their antenna — it came equally from all directions. Simultaneously, Princeton physicists predicted exactly such radiation from the Big Bang.

faq.question: What can CMB temperature fluctuations tell us?
faq.answer: The pattern of hot and cold spots reveals the universe's geometry (flat), age (~13.8 billion years), composition (proportions of matter, dark matter, dark energy), expansion rate, and the seeds from which all cosmic structure grew. The CMB is the most information-rich observation in cosmology.
